title: Browser Isolation & CSP: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on the same-origin policy beyond fetch, iframes and sandbox, clickjacking defences, postMessage safety and Content Security Policy basics.

chapters.title: Same-Origin Policy Beyond fetch
points: Origin = scheme + host + port; all three must match, so http://a.com, https://a.com and https://a.com:8443 are three different origins
SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses, not sending requests: cross-origin form posts, img/script/link tags and simple GETs still go out, so CSRF tokens are still required
SOP also covers DOM access (window/iframe contentWindow), localStorage/IndexedDB (per-origin) and canvas tainting by cross-origin images; cookies use host+path, not origin, and ignore port and scheme
Relaxing it: CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin, server opt-in to let JS read the response); document.domain is deprecated, so use postMessage or CORS
Mental model: embedding (script, img, iframe) is allowed, reading is denied by default; a preflight OPTIONS is sent for non-simple requests, and a wildcard * cannot be combined with credentials

chapters.title: Iframes and the sandbox Attribute
points: <iframe sandbox> with no value applies every restriction: unique opaque origin, no scripts, no forms, no popups, no top navigation, no plugins
Tokens re-enable single features: allow-scripts, allow-forms, allow-popups, allow-modals, allow-same-origin, allow-top-navigation, allow-downloads
Example for untrusted widgets: <iframe sandbox="allow-scripts" src="https://widget.example"></iframe>, which can run JS but has an opaque origin with no cookies or storage access

Comparison: sandbox without allow-same-origin keeps the frame isolated; allow-scripts plus allow-same-origin on a same-origin srcdoc/src lets the frame remove its own sandbox attribute, so it is useless
Use the allow attribute (Permissions Policy) for camera, geolocation and fullscreen, and add referrerpolicy and loading="lazy" on embeds

chapters.title: Clickjacking: X-Frame-Options vs frame-ancestors
points: Clickjacking = attacker frames your page invisibly (opacity:0 iframe) under a decoy button so the victim's click lands on your UI with their session cookies
X-Frame-Options accepts only DENY or SAMEORIGIN (ALLOW-FROM is obsolete and ignored by modern browsers), it is a header only and can't whitelist multiple origins
CSP frame-ancestors accepts 'none', 'self' and a list of origins or wildcards (frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.com), and it is the modern replacement
When both are present, browsers that support CSP frame-ancestors ignore X-Frame-Options; send both for old-browser coverage
Mistakes: frame-ancestors in a <meta> tag is ignored (header only), and frame-src/child-src control what YOU embed, not who embeds you; SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies also reduce clickjacking impact

chapters.title: postMessage and Origin Checks
points: Send: targetWindow.postMessage(data, 'https://app.example'); the second argument is targetOrigin, and '*' leaks data to whatever page is loaded in that window

Receive: window.addEventListener('message', e => { if (e.origin !== 'https://app.example') return; ... }); check e.origin exactly, never indexOf/endsWith/regex substrings (evil-app.example.com bypasses endsWith)
e.origin is set by the browser and can't be forged, but e.data is attacker-controlled: validate its shape and type, and never pass it to innerHTML, eval or location
Also check e.source === expectedWindow when multiple frames are listening, because origin alone doesn't tell you which frame sent it

Mistakes: no origin check at all, a '*' targetOrigin when sending secrets, trusting 'null' origin (sandboxed or data: frames send 'null'), and treating a message as authenticated when it is only origin-checked

chapters.title: Content Security Policy Basics
points: CSP is a response header (Content-Security-Policy) listing allowed sources per directive: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' https://cdn.example; img-src * data:; object-src 'none'
Key directives: default-src (fallback), script-src, style-src, img-src, connect-src (fetch/XHR/WebSocket), frame-src, frame-ancestors, base-uri, form-action

Inline scripts and eval are blocked unless allowed: use a per-response nonce (script-src 'nonce-R4nd0m') or a hash ('sha256-...'), and avoid 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval', which defeat the XSS protection; 'strict-dynamic' trusts scripts loaded by a nonced script

Rollout: use Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only with report-to/report-uri first, read violations, then enforce; the nonce must be new on every response, and a CSP is defence in depth, not a replacement for output encoding

Mistakes: wildcard or whole-CDN allowlists (JSONP/Angular gadgets bypass), omitting object-src and base-uri (allows injection bypass), reusing a static nonce, and forgetting that default-src does not cover frame-ancestors, base-uri or form-action

chapters.title: Browser Isolation Cheat Sheet
points: SOP: scheme+host+port match; blocks reads, not sends; CORS opts in; keep CSRF tokens
Iframe: sandbox="" locks everything, add tokens one by one; never combine allow-scripts with allow-same-origin on same-origin content
Anti-clickjack header: Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or 'self'), plus X-Frame-Options: DENY (or SAMEORIGIN) for legacy browsers
postMessage: send with an exact targetOrigin, receive with exact e.origin ===, check e.source, treat e.data as untrusted input
CSP starter: default-src 'self'; script-src 'nonce-…' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; test with Report-Only first
